These criteria were designed to select individuals who could provide detailed, first-hand accounts of ADHD-related experiences in team dynamics and marketing innovation. To ensure the accuracy of the ADHD diagnosis, participants were asked to provide confirmation of their formal diagnosis (e.g., a medical certificate or psychological report) or to consent to contact a relevant professional. This process allowed us to ensure the validity of participants’ ADHD status and to avoid biases resulting from self-diagnosis.

The study’s inclusion criteria were designed to include both individuals with ADHD and individuals with diverse organizational roles, industries, and geographic regions. Table 1 shows the inclusion criteria and their rationale:

In total, more than 50 responses to the initial calls were received. After careful consideration of the inclusion criteria and confirmation of the ADHD diagnosis, the final sample consisted of 35 participants, drawn from six countries: Iran ( n = 8), the United States ( n = 7), India ( n = 6), Brazil ( n = 5), the Netherlands ( n = 5), and Japan ( n = 4). Of these, 21 (60.0%) were from developed markets, and 14 (40.0%) were from emerging markets. The sample consisted of 15 marketing managers (42.9%), 12 marketing team members (34.3%), and 8 freelancers/consultants (22.9%), who were selected to provide sufficient diversity in work experiences and contexts and to allow for in-depth data analysis, in line with the recommendations of Eisenhardt and Graebner (2007) . This geographic and occupational diversity was intended to broaden the contextual diversity of participants’ work experiences and to examine whether emerging theoretical concepts and relationships were also observed across different organizational and national contexts. The selection of countries was not done with the aim of achieving national representation or making systematic comparisons between countries; rather, the diversity of institutional and cultural contexts was used to strengthen theoretical sampling and explore and enrich emerging categories.

Data were collected through 45- to 90-min semi-structured interviews, conducted online via Google Meet. Interviews were recorded and transcribed with informed consent from participants. The interview protocol was structured in three parts: (1) a demographic questionnaire to capture baseline information, (2) semi-structured questions about experiences related to neurodiversity, collaboration in marketing teams, customer-oriented interactions, and boundary-setting activities, and (3) follow-up questions to deepen and clarify experiences and perspectives raised during the interviews.

Given the international nature of the sample and potential differences in the equivalence and understanding of specialized concepts related to ADHD, neurodiversity, team dynamics, innovation, and customer-oriented interactions, all interviews were conducted in English. English was chosen as the common language of the study to avoid semantic differences resulting from translation and reinterpretation of specialized concepts in the data collection and analysis process. Therefore, none of the interviews were translated for the purposes of analysis, and data analysis was conducted directly based on the original English transcripts. In cases where participants’ responses contained ambiguous phrases or concepts, follow-up questions were used to clarify their intended meaning.

The demographic characteristics, professional role, ADHD status, and geographic distribution of participants are presented in Table 2 . Participants included individuals with a formal diagnosis of ADHD and individuals without ADHD who had direct professional experience working with colleagues or team members with ADHD. This diversity allowed for constant comparison of narratives and examination of similarities, differences, and contextual conditions related to emerging themes.

Informed consent was obtained from all participants before the interviews. They were assured that their identities and personal information would remain confidential and that the data would only be used for research purposes. For participants who reported a formal ADHD diagnosis, diagnostic verification was used to distinguish formally diagnosed participants from participants without ADHD and to reduce reliance on self-diagnosis. Also, to increase data validity, triangulation was used: supplementary information was collected from public sources (such as participants’ LinkedIn profiles or organizational websites) and, in 5 cases, interviews with colleagues or team members were conducted to provide additional perspectives on ADHD-related experiences, team interactions, and work practices. To ensure the quality of the sample and its appropriateness for scientific evaluations, the following measures were implemented:

Confirmation of ADHD diagnosis and participant ADHD status: The sample included both participants with a formal ADHD diagnosis and participants without ADHD. Among the 35 participants, 19 had a formal ADHD diagnosis, and 16 did not. Participants with a formal ADHD diagnosis were asked to provide official diagnostic documentation or to consent to confirmation according to the study’s eligibility procedure. Participants without ADHD were included when they had relevant professional experience working with, supervising, or collaborating with colleagues or team members with ADHD. The inclusion of participants without ADHD was intentional and was designed to capture workplace perspectives beyond first-person accounts. These participants had direct professional experience working with colleagues or team members with ADHD and were therefore able to provide observations concerning team interactions, work practices, collaboration, and organizational responses to ADHD-related characteristics. Participants with ADHD, in contrast, provided first-person accounts of their own experiences. These two perspectives were distinguished during data collection and subsequent analysis rather than being treated as analytically equivalent.

Diversity of participant perspectives: The sample was intentionally heterogeneous in terms of professional role, ADHD status, industry context, and geographic background. The inclusion of both participants with ADHD and participants without ADHD who had direct workplace experience with colleagues with ADHD enabled comparison across different experiential positions. Diversity in professional roles, industries, and geographic contexts was used to examine whether emerging categories remained relevant across different conditions rather than to establish statistical generalizability ( Eisenhardt and Graebner, 2007 ).

Theoretical saturation: Theoretical saturation was not defined by a fixed, predetermined number of interviews, but rather was assessed using specific analytical criteria during simultaneous data collection and analysis, constant comparative analysis, and theoretical note-taking. Saturation was considered achieved when successive interviews: (1) did not generate new and meaningful conceptual codes; (2) did not add new features or dimensions to existing categories; (3) did not reveal new theoretical relationships between categories; and (4) did not fundamentally change the context, implications, or theoretical explanations of the core categories. These criteria were continually checked against new data and theoretical notes. With the six core categories established and the gradual decline of new theoretical information observed, the final six interviews were specifically examined as saturation confirmation interviews. Data from these interviews were compared with existing codes and categories to determine whether they generated new codes, features, dimensions, conditions, or theoretical relationships. These interviews largely resulted in repetition or enrichment of existing categories and did not generate new, substantive theoretical insights. Data collection was therefore stopped because the original categories had reached a sufficient level of theoretical development and the new data no longer provided meaningful changes to the theoretical structure or explanation. Consequently, the decision to saturate was made based on the reduction of new theoretical information and the consolidation of categories, rather than simply on achieving a predetermined sample size.

Transparency of the process: All steps in the selection of participants, including contacting support organizations and reviewing responses, were fully documented to ensure the replicability and transparency of the research.

Data collection and analysis were conducted simultaneously, following the logic of classical grounded theory ( Glaser, 1998 ). The analysis process involved open, selective, and theoretical coding, with constant comparative analysis and theoretical note-taking throughout the research process. Rather than following a strictly linear sequence, the researchers iteratively moved between interview transcripts, initial codes, emerging categories, and theoretical insights. In the open coding phase, 304 codes were extracted from the interview transcripts. Then, through continuous comparison of codes in terms of conceptual similarities and differences, characteristics, conditions of emergence, and their relationship to the phenomenon under study, related codes were gradually grouped into 14 subcategories. Codes that referred to a common concept or process were grouped into a subcategory; subcategories that had meaningful conceptual overlap or theoretical connections were then compared with each other and merged into higher-order categories. In this process, integration was not based solely on the number or frequency of codes, but rather on the conceptual coherence, explanatory power, and relevance of the code set to the emerging theoretical process.

Next, 14 subcategories were compared and merged based on their conceptual features and theoretical relevance, resulting in the formation of six main categories. Selective coding focused the analysis on the categories that were most relevant to the emerging theoretical explanation; then, theoretical coding examined the relationships among the six main categories, resulting in the formation of three theoretical codes. Thus, the analytical path from the initial 304 codes to the 14 subcategories, six main categories, and three theoretical codes was iterative and grounded theory, and did not follow a predetermined classification system.

Constant comparative analysis and theoretical note-taking were used throughout these steps to refine the categories, identify their features and conditions, and guide subsequent data collection. Theoretical notes included emerging concepts, features, conditions, analytic comparisons, theoretical questions, and decisions to conduct further interviews. Narratives from participants with ADHD were also consistently compared with those from participants without ADHD who had direct professional experience working with colleagues or team members with ADHD. Similarities, differences, and conflicting narratives were used to refine the features and conditions of emerging categories.

Data coding and interpretation were conducted collaboratively by three researchers. Analytical disagreements were discussed and resolved through re-comparison with the original transcripts and analytical notes. Atlas.ti software was used to organize transcripts, codes, and analytic records; however, conceptual and theoretical decisions were made by the researchers.

Given the interpretive nature of grounded theory research, the researchers recognized that their disciplinary backgrounds, prior assumptions, and interpretations could shape data collection, coding, constant comparison, and theoretical development. Reflexivity was therefore maintained throughout the research process through continuous memoing and discussion among the three researchers. During coding, emerging interpretations were repeatedly compared with the original interview transcripts and analytic memos to distinguish participants’ accounts from researchers’ interpretations. Differences in interpretation were discussed collaboratively and resolved through repeated examination of the underlying data rather than through reliance on a predetermined coding framework. The researchers also remained attentive to the possibility of interpreting ADHD-related characteristics primarily through a strengths-based perspective and therefore deliberately considered contradictory and challenging accounts, including impulsivity, distraction, stress, anxiety, communication difficulties, and social isolation. This reflexive process helped maintain alignment between the emerging theoretical framework and participants’ accounts.

After the initial interview, the researcher began conducting interviews and open coding, transcribing and coding each interview as it was completed. Coding, as highlighted by Coyne and Cowley (2006) , is a dynamic and reflexive process that involves assigning initial conceptual labels to the data ( Coyne and Cowley, 2006 ; Glaser, 1998 ). Alongside data collection, the team conducted constant comparative analysis and memoing, which are integral components of grounded theory ( Chun Tie et al., 2019 ). It is worth noting that these two activities were applied continuously throughout the research and were not limited to this specific phase. Through open coding, we identified 304 codes, which we then organized into 14 subcategories and six core categories. A sample of interviews and their initial codes is presented in Table 4 .

Table 4 illustrates how participants’ own accounts were translated into initial open codes. The excerpts include both enabling and challenging experiences of ADHD in the workplace. Participants described creativity, divergent thinking, resilience, and adaptability, but also reported impulsive decision-making, distraction, stress and anxiety, communication difficulties, social isolation, and structural barriers. Thus, the coding process did not assume ADHD-related characteristics to be inherently positive or negative; rather, both dimensions emerged from participants’ accounts.

Glaser (1978) describes selective coding as a stage in which coding is limited to only those categories relevant to the research problem ( Glaser, 1978 ). This process continues until both the main category and related categories reach saturation. Examples of open codes and their classifications, along with the results of selective coding, is presented in Table 5 .

Selective coding consolidated the open codes into six main categories: Cognitive Dynamics and Neurodiverse Creativity, Synergistic Connections, Customer-Oriented Neurodiverse Dynamics, Resilient Adaptability, Structured Constructs, and External Validation. These categories captured both enabling and constraining dimensions of participants’ experiences. Creativity, divergent thinking, intense focus, adaptability, and resilience were described as potential resources, whereas communication difficulties, systemic barriers, distraction, stress and anxiety, and the need for organizational support reflected challenges that could constrain performance. The resulting categories therefore represent the conditions under which ADHD-related characteristics may support or hinder workplace functioning.

Theoretical coding integrated the six main categories into higher-order concepts and clarified their relationships within the emerging grounded theory ( Glaser, 1978 ; Evans, 2013 ). This process resulted in three theoretical codes—Neurodiverse Cognitive Synergy, Mediated Empathy in Boundary-Spanning, and Resilient Organizational Adaptation—which capture the relationships among the main categories identified through selective coding. Specifically, Neurodiverse Cognitive Synergy integrates Cognitive Dynamics and Neurodiverse Creativity with Customer-Oriented Neurodiverse Dynamics; Mediated Empathy in Boundary-Spanning connects Synergistic Connections with External Validation; and Resilient Organizational Adaptation integrates Resilient Adaptability with Structured Constructs. These theoretical codes are presented in Table 6 .

The three theoretical codes formed an interconnected framework emerging from the interview data. Neurodiverse Cognitive Synergy captures how ADHD-related cognitive characteristics, including divergent thinking and intense focus, intersect with role adaptation and customer-oriented interactions. Mediated Empathy in Boundary-Spanning describes how communication and relational barriers between team members and across organizational and customer boundaries can be addressed through practices such as team transparency, communication protocols, feedback, and organizational support. Participants associated these practices with improved collaboration, reduced misunderstandings, stronger role alignment, and more effective customer-oriented interactions. Resilient Organizational Adaptation captures how individuals and teams respond to challenges such as distraction, stress, anxiety, and changing work demands through organizational tools, flexibility, and support. Together, these relationships support the model derived from the data ( Figure 2 ) by presenting the following fundamental theory.

Participants’ accounts suggest that “neurocognitive synergy and Mediated Empathy in Boundary-Spanning may be associated with resilient organizational adaptation in marketing teams and may support customer-oriented innovation under enabling organizational conditions.”

Figure 2 provides a visual representation of the grounded theory derived from the three theoretical codes of the study and depicts the relationships among them as interconnected and non-linear. At the center of the model, Neurodiverse Cognitive Synergy represents the cognitive synergy emerging from the interaction between ADHD-related characteristics, role demands, and customer-oriented contexts. This component comprises Cognitive Dynamics, Neurodiverse Creativity, and Customer-Oriented Neurodiverse Dynamics. The findings indicate that divergent thinking, risk-taking and impulsivity, and intense focus may function as potential resources for creativity and problem-solving under appropriate conditions, while their effectiveness remains contingent upon role fit and contextual conditions ( Wiklund et al., 2016 ; Lerner et al., 2019 ; Hatak et al., 2021 ).

The surrounding layer, Mediated Empathy in Boundary-Spanning, represents the relational and interactional processes through which cognitive differences are translated into effective collaboration and interaction across team, organizational, and customer boundaries. Within this layer, External Validation comprises Organizational Support and Identity and Self-Confidence, highlighting the role of organizational support, feedback, and inclusive practices in strengthening participation and self-confidence. Synergistic Connections, in turn, comprises Team Collaboration, Communication Challenges, and Systemic Barriers, reflecting both opportunities for collaboration and the communication and organizational frictions identified in the data. Thus, mediated empathy refers to a relational process through which actors coordinate different perspectives and ways of working and transform these differences into workable forms of collaboration.

The upper layer, Resilient Organizational Adaptation, represents the organizational and individual mechanisms required to sustain and facilitate these processes and consists of Resilient Adaptability and Structured Constructs. Resilient Adaptability, represented by Resilience to Challenges and Stress and Anxiety Management, reflects the capacity to respond and adapt to workplace pressures and challenges. Structured Constructs, represented by Organizational Tools and Distraction Management, refers to the structures and tools that provide the stability and scaffolding required for effective functioning. This distinction suggests that realizing neurodiverse capabilities depends not only on individual adaptability but also on the alignment of organizational structures and support mechanisms with individual needs ( Austin and Pisano, 2017 ; Hatak et al., 2021 ).

Overall, as indicated by Interconnected, Not Linear in the figure, the three theoretical codes should not be interpreted as sequential stages or linear causal relationships; rather, they dynamically interact with and mutually reinforce and shape one another. Accordingly, Neurodiverse Cognitive Synergy, Mediated Empathy in Boundary-Spanning, and Resilient Organizational Adaptation jointly shape the conditions under which ADHD-related cognitive capabilities may, depending on relational contexts, role demands, and organizational structures, be translated into creativity, adaptability, and customer-oriented interactions. The proposed model therefore avoids attributing innovation directly to individual ADHD characteristics and instead emphasizes the context-dependent and interactive process through which neurodiverse capabilities may be realized within marketing teams.

This study contributes to the emerging literature on neurodiversity, marketing management, and organizational psychology by developing an exploratory, data-grounded framework connecting ADHD-related workplace experiences with customer-oriented work and innovation in marketing teams. The study addresses an underexplored intersection of ADHD, neurodiversity, marketing teams, customer-facing work, and organizational innovation. Drawing on qualitative accounts, the framework integrates three theoretical codes—Neurodiverse Cognitive Synergy, Mediated Empathy in Boundary-Spanning, and Resilient Organizational Adaptation—to explain how individual characteristics, interpersonal processes, and organizational conditions may interact in neurodiverse marketing environments. The contribution of the framework lies not in proposing that ADHD inherently produces innovation, but in showing how ADHD-related characteristics may become resources or challenges depending on task demands, role fit, interpersonal dynamics, and organizational support. This contextual interpretation extends the neurodiversity paradigm ( Fletcher-Watson, 2022 ; Apperly et al., 2024 ) and complements person-environment fit theory ( Kristof-Brown et al., 2005 ) by shifting attention from individual characteristics alone toward the organizational conditions under which those characteristics are experienced and utilized. It also responds to calls for greater attention to neurodiversity in organizational and marketing contexts ( van Rijswijk et al., 2024a ; Go Jefferies and Ahmed, 2022 ).

Neurodiverse Cognitive Synergy represents the first theoretical code. It captures participants’ accounts of divergent thinking, creativity, risk-taking, and intense focus in relation to creative and customer-oriented activities. This finding is consistent with research linking ADHD-related characteristics to entrepreneurship and creative activity ( Wiklund et al., 2016 ; Lerner et al., 2019 ). Hatak et al. (2021) further demonstrate that the relationship between ADHD symptoms and entrepreneurial performance is contingent on other individual and contextual factors. The present study extends this contextual perspective from individual entrepreneurship to marketing-team processes by suggesting that cognitive differences may contribute to idea generation and customer-oriented problem solving when supported by appropriate roles and team arrangements. At the same time, the findings complicate a purely strengths-based interpretation. Participants also described impulsive decisions, distraction, stress, communication difficulties, and social isolation. For example, one participant reported that “my extreme impulsivity has led me to make several poor decisions in marketing campaigns,” while another stated, “In busy meetings, I feel isolated because I cannot keep up with the pace of the discussions.” These contrasting accounts suggest that the same ADHD-related characteristics may have divergent consequences across situations. Thus, the theoretical contribution of Neurodiverse Cognitive Synergy lies not in labeling ADHD characteristics as strengths, but in explaining their potentially contingent value within particular work contexts.

Mediated Empathy in Boundary-Spanning represents the relational dimension of the framework. It describes how communication and relational barriers associated with differences in work styles may be addressed through organizational support, structured communication, feedback, and interaction with internal and external stakeholders. Boundary-spanning activities are relevant because they connect team members with customers and other organizational actors and can facilitate the exchange of information and social resources ( Bettencourt and Brown, 2003 ; Fredrickson, 2001 ; Wiklund et al., 2017 ). The concept also complements research on collective emotional intelligence ( Curseu et al., 2015 ) by emphasizing that effective relational processes may depend not only on individual interpersonal capabilities but also on the structures through which interactions are organized.

Importantly, mediated empathy does not imply that individuals with ADHD inherently possess greater empathy or emotional intelligence. Rather, the concept refers to the processes through which empathy and mutual understanding may be facilitated when organizational practices reduce communication barriers and provide opportunities for clarification, feedback, and reciprocal adjustment. This interpretation is particularly relevant given participants’ reports of misunderstandings and social isolation alongside accounts of empathy and interpersonal engagement.

Resilient Organizational Adaptation represents the organizational dimension of the framework. Participants described the importance of role fit, autonomy, structured tools, feedback, and environmental support in managing ADHD-related challenges. This finding is consistent with person-environment fit theory ( Kristof-Brown et al., 2005 ) and previous research emphasizing the importance of contextual conditions in understanding ADHD-related work and entrepreneurial outcomes ( Verheul et al., 2015 ; Hatak et al., 2021 ). One participant explained, “If I am placed in the wrong role, I cannot adapt to the work environment, and therefore I am more likely to seek a job where I have more control over my environment.” This account illustrates that adaptation is not necessarily an individual responsibility; it may also involve organizational design, including flexibility, structured support, and appropriate allocation of responsibilities.

Taken together, the three theoretical codes suggest a multi-level process linking cognitive characteristics, relational processes, and organizational conditions. Neurodiverse Cognitive Synergy concerns the potential contribution of cognitive differences to creative and customer-oriented work; Mediated Empathy in Boundary-Spanning concerns the relational mechanisms through which differences can be negotiated; and Resilient Organizational Adaptation concerns the organizational structures that enable individuals and teams to manage these differences. The resulting framework therefore connects the individual, relational, and organizational levels rather than treating ADHD as an isolated individual characteristic.

This interpretation also contributes to marketing literature by connecting neurodiversity with organizational creativity ( Amabile, 1996 ) and open innovation ( Chesbrough, 2003 ). Neurodiverse Cognitive Synergy can complement creativity perspectives by highlighting how cognitive differences may contribute to idea generation, while Mediated Empathy in Boundary-Spanning connects neurodiverse team members with customers and other external stakeholders. These connections are theoretical extensions generated from the qualitative findings rather than empirical tests of the underlying creativity or open-innovation theories. The framework consequently offers a promising starting point for future research. Rather than claiming that ADHD causes innovation, it proposes that ADHD-related characteristics, relational processes, and organizational supports may form a configuration through which innovative potential can be realized in some marketing contexts. This proposition is consistent with prior research showing that ADHD-related characteristics can have both productive and challenging consequences depending on contextual conditions ( Wiklund et al., 2016 ; Lerner et al., 2019 ; Hatak et al., 2021 ).

The findings also highlight several theoretical directions. First, cultural context may influence how ADHD-related characteristics are interpreted, disclosed, and supported. Because the present sample includes participants from multiple national contexts but is not designed for systematic cross-cultural comparison, the framework should not be assumed to operate uniformly across cultures. Second, the focus on ADHD means that the applicability of the framework to autism, dyslexia, dyspraxia, or other forms of neurodivergence remains an empirical question. Future research could examine whether the three theoretical codes are ADHD-specific or whether they can be adapted across neurodevelopmental conditions. Longitudinal and mixed-method research could further examine whether the relationships proposed by the framework are sustained over time and whether they are associated with observable outcomes such as innovation participation, team performance, retention, or inclusion.

This study also offers practical implications for marketing managers, HR professionals, and organizations seeking to develop more inclusive customer-oriented teams. Because the framework is exploratory, these implications should be viewed as context-sensitive organizational practices rather than empirically validated interventions.

First, organizations can combine flexibility with structure. Participants described potential benefits associated with creativity, divergent thinking, and intense focus, but also challenges involving distraction, impulsivity, stress, and workload management. Structured tools such as written instructions, task division, visual aids, time blocking, team dashboards, and appropriate digital systems may provide useful scaffolding ( Chien et al., 2021 ).

Second, organizations can design roles around individual person-environment fit rather than assumptions about ADHD. Flexible responsibilities, opportunities for creative work, and greater control over task execution may benefit some employees, while others may prefer greater structure. The findings therefore support individualized job design rather than a standardized “ADHD role.”

Third, managers can strengthen feedback, communication, and relational support. Participants described both interpersonal strengths and communication difficulties. Regular feedback, transparent communication, written follow-up after meetings, and psychologically supportive team environments may help reduce misunderstandings and facilitate collaboration.

Fourth, organizations should adopt a balanced strengths-and-support approach. The findings do not suggest that organizations should simply “leverage ADHD strengths.” Instead, inclusion requires recognizing potential capabilities while also addressing challenges such as impulsivity, distraction, anxiety, stress, and social isolation. This balanced approach is particularly important because the same characteristic may function differently across roles and situations.

Finally, the findings suggest that neuroinclusion may be particularly relevant to customer-facing and boundary-spanning work, where diverse perspectives can interact with customer needs. However, organizations should not assume that employees with ADHD are naturally better suited to customer-facing or creative roles. Such assignments should be based on individual preferences, capabilities, and job requirements.

This study has several limitations that should be considered when interpreting the proposed framework. First, the sample size and purposive recruitment strategy are appropriate for grounded theory development but do not support statistical generalization. The recruitment process may also have introduced self-selection bias. Individuals who were particularly interested in neurodiversity, had salient workplace experiences of ADHD, or felt more comfortable discussing their experiences may have been more likely to participate. Consequently, the accounts may not fully represent individuals with less salient, less positive, or more difficult workplace experiences.

Second, the cultural composition of the sample may limit transferability across national contexts. Although participants were recruited from multiple countries, approximately 60% were from developed-market contexts. Organizational practices, attitudes toward hierarchy, disclosure, disability, and neurodiversity may vary across institutional and cultural environments. The findings should therefore not be interpreted as culturally universal. Future comparative research could examine whether the three theoretical codes operate differently across developed and emerging economies and across cultures with different expectations regarding hierarchy, autonomy, and disclosure.

Third, the study focuses specifically on ADHD and should not be generalized to neurodiversity as a whole. Autism, dyslexia, dyspraxia, and other neurodevelopmental conditions may involve different workplace experiences, support requirements, and patterns of strengths and challenges. Future research should examine whether the proposed framework is condition-specific or can be extended, with appropriate modification, to other neurodevelopmental conditions.

Fourth, ADHD may co-occur with other conditions that influence workplace experiences. The present study does not allow the independent contribution of ADHD to be separated from possible co-occurring conditions or individual differences. Future studies could explicitly examine how co-occurring conditions and other individual characteristics shape the relationships proposed in the framework.

Fifth, researcher subjectivity is an inherent consideration in grounded theory research. Although reflexive discussions, memoing, and collaborative comparison were used to reduce the influence of individual interpretations, researcher subjectivity cannot be eliminated in an interpretive grounded theory study. Future studies could strengthen the framework through independent coding, multiple researchers, triangulation with observations or organizational records, and mixed-method designs.

Sixth, the cross-sectional nature of the study limits conclusions about long-term organizational outcomes. The proposed framework identifies relationships among cognitive characteristics, relational processes, organizational support, and adaptation, but it does not establish whether these processes persist over time or whether supportive practices produce sustained changes in innovation, performance, retention, or inclusion. Longitudinal research could therefore examine how these relationships develop across different stages of employment and organizational change.

Seventh, confidentiality and stigma may have influenced participants’ accounts. Participants may have been reluctant to disclose experiences involving impairment, interpersonal conflict, failed decisions, anxiety, or negative workplace consequences when disclosure could carry social or professional risks. Conversely, participants who were more comfortable discussing neurodiversity may have emphasized particular aspects of their experiences. These possibilities should be considered when interpreting both positive and negative accounts.

Finally, the qualitative nature of the study means that the proposed relationships have not been empirically validated as causal relationships. The framework should therefore be understood as a theory-generating proposition that identifies potentially important relationships and conditions for further investigation. Future research could test these propositions using larger and more diverse samples, cross-cultural comparisons, longitudinal designs, and mixed methods.

Using a grounded theory approach, this study develops an exploratory, theory-generating frameworkneurodiversity, marketing managementfor understanding how ADHD-related workplace experiences may interact with marketing team processes and customer-oriented innovation. The findings identify three theoretical codes, Neurodiverse Cognitive Synergy, Mediated Empathy in Boundary-Spanning, and Resilient Organizational Adaptation, that capture patterned relationships across participants’ accounts.

The findings do not support a simple strengths-based or deficit-based interpretation of ADHD. Rather, participants described both potential resources, including divergent thinking, creativity, intense focus, adaptability, and risk-taking, and challenges involving impulsivity, distraction, stress, anxiety, communication difficulties, and social isolation. The findings therefore suggest that the consequences of ADHD-related characteristics are conditional and shaped partly by task demands, role fit, interpersonal relationships, and organizational support.

From a theoretical perspective, the study extends existing discussions of neurodiversity, person-environment fit, organizational creativity, and boundary-spanning by connecting individual characteristics with relational and organizational processes. Its principal contribution is not to demonstrate that ADHD causes innovation, but to propose a data-grounded framework for examining the conditions under which ADHD-related characteristics may be productively utilized in marketing teams. This interpretation is consistent with prior research showing that ADHD-related characteristics can have both enabling and constraining consequences and that their relationship with performance depends on contextual configurations ( Wiklund et al., 2016 ; Lerner et al., 2019 ; Hatak et al., 2021 ).

Practically, the findings suggest that organizations may consider combining autonomy and flexibility with structured support, transparent communication, supportive feedback, and appropriate role alignment. These implications should be understood as context-sensitive organizational design considerations rather than validated interventions. Inclusive management should recognize variation among employees with ADHD rather than assuming that all individuals share the same strengths or support needs.

The study is subject to limitations concerning sample size, self-selection bias, cultural composition, the exclusive focus on ADHD, possible co-occurring conditions, researcher subjectivity, cross-sectional design, confidentiality, and stigma. These limitations constrain the generalizability and causal interpretation of the framework. Future research should therefore test and refine the proposed relationships using larger, more culturally diverse samples; longitudinal and mixed-methods designs; and comparisons across neurodevelopmental conditions and organizational contexts.

Ultimately, this study invites researchers and organizations to move beyond both purely deficit-based and overly celebratory accounts of ADHD. Rather than treating neurodiversity as inherently beneficial or problematic, the findings suggest examining how organizational conditions shape how neurodivergent characteristics are experienced and utilized. In this sense, the framework offers a starting point for further empirical investigation into neuroinclusive marketing teams and the organizational conditions that may support innovation.
